transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in today?

Hi. Um… I guess the thing that finally made me book the appointment is this pattern I keep running into at work. I’m an accountant, and after audits or sometimes after mentorship events, there are always follow-up items—emails to send, review notes to finalize, forms that need to be completed—and I start them with every intention of finishing them. I really do.

But then a few days later I’ll realize the final email never actually went out, or the review note is still sitting half-done, or the form didn’t get submitted. And it’s not that I don’t care or that I’m trying to avoid it. It’s more like I begin the process, think I’m on track, and somehow the last step just… doesn’t happen. Then I’m embarrassed because it looks careless, and I have to go back and fix something that should have been simple. That’s what pushed me to come in.
When you realize these tasks haven’t been completed, how do you typically feel about it? Does it affect your mood or energy level?

I’m not sure I’ve really tracked it in a clean way, honestly. In the moment when I notice it, I mostly feel this kind of sinking embarrassment, like, “Oh no, not again,” and then I get very focused on trying to patch it up quickly so it doesn’t look as bad.

As far as mood or energy… I mean, it’s frustrating, and I can be hard on myself about it. Sometimes it kind of hangs over me for a bit because I’m replaying how I missed something that should have been straightforward. But I don’t know if I’d say I’ve noticed a clear pattern like it completely changes my mood for the day or anything. It’s more this immediate wave of shame and irritation with myself, and then I’m scrambling to fix it.
Have you ever experienced periods where you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in things for more than a couple of weeks at a time?

I don’t think so… at least not in a way I’ve clearly identified. I mean, I’ve definitely had stretches where I felt discouraged or worn down, especially when I’m behind on things or feeling like I’ve disappointed someone, and I can get pretty self-critical. But when you say “down or hopeless for more than a couple of weeks,” I’m not sure I’d say that fits.

And losing interest in things… I don’t know. I haven’t really noticed a period where everything felt pointless or where I stopped caring about things across the board. It’s more situational, I think? Like I’ll feel bad when I’ve messed something up, and then I kind of stew on it or feel embarrassed. But I can’t point to a solid two-week period where I was just consistently hopeless or uninterested.
Have you ever had days where you felt down or sad most of the time, even when there wasn’t a specific reason like missing a task or disappointing someone?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I’ve had bad days, definitely. Days where I wake up already feeling kind of heavy or irritated or just… not great. But when I try to separate that from something that happened, it’s hard, because usually if I look closely there’s some reason in the background, like I’m behind on something or I’m worried I forgot something or I feel like I’m not keeping up.

I don’t think I’ve noticed days where I’m just sad most of the time for no identifiable reason. Or if I have, I haven’t been paying attention to it in that way. I’m usually trying to figure out what caused it, and then I end up tying it back to some mistake or pressure or unfinished thing.

So I guess my answer is… not that I can clearly point to. I don’t want to say “never,” because maybe I’m not the best observer of myself, but I haven’t noticed a pattern of being down all day out of nowhere.
Have you ever noticed a time when you weren’t able to enjoy things that usually make you happy, even when things were going well or there was no obvious reason for it?

I’m not sure I can think of a clear example of that. I mean, I’ve had times where I didn’t feel like doing something I normally enjoy because I was tired, or distracted, or I had this nagging sense that I should be doing something more productive. Like even if I’m technically relaxing, part of my brain is still sort of scanning for what I forgot or what’s due next, so I might not be fully enjoying it.

But if you mean more like… things were basically fine, no obvious stressor, and suddenly the usual things just didn’t feel good or enjoyable for a while, I don’t think I’ve really noticed that. Or at least I haven’t recognized it as its own separate thing. Usually if I’m not enjoying something, I can tie it to being preoccupied or feeling behind or guilty, not that the thing itself stopped being enjoyable.

So I guess I’d say no, not in a way I can clearly point to. It’s more like my mind gets in the way of enjoying things sometimes, rather than me feeling unable to enjoy anything for no reason.

Can you tell me about a time when you successfully completed a task from start to finish without any issues? How did that process feel different, if at all, compared to the tasks you end up leaving unfinished?

I think when I complete something start to finish without problems, it’s usually because it’s very contained and there’s a clear end point right in front of me. Like if I’m in the middle of an audit and I’m working through a specific section, and I can see exactly what has to be checked and documented, I can sometimes get into a rhythm and finish it. It feels… almost relieving, like I’m just following the track and I don’t have to keep re-deciding what to do next.

Where it goes wrong is more with the follow-up pieces afterward. That’s actually part of what pushed me to make this appointment. I’ll come out of an audit, or even a mentorship event, with every intention of finishing the follow-up. I’ll start the final email, or I’ll start drafting the review note, or I’ll open the form I need to submit, and in my mind it’s basically “in progress,” so I feel like I’m handling it.

But then a few days later I’ll realize the final version never got sent, or the note never got finalized, or the form is still sitting there incomplete. And it’s not that I didn’t care about it. I absolutely intended to finish it. Sometimes I even remember doing part of it so clearly that I almost assume it must be done, and then I check and realize, no, I only started it.

So the difference is that the completed tasks feel like there was a continuous line from beginning to end. The unfinished ones feel like I got 80 or 90 percent of the way there, but the last step somehow fell out of view. And honestly it’s embarrassing, because these are not huge impossible tasks. They’re things I know how to do. That’s what makes it so frustrating.
Can you tell me if there are times when you have trouble even starting tasks, not just finishing them? Like, you know you need to do something but you can’t seem to get yourself to begin?

I’m actually not sure how to answer that cleanly. I can think of times where I delay starting something, definitely, but I’m not always sure whether that’s “can’t start” or just… I’m avoiding it, or I’m tired, or I’m waiting until I feel like I know exactly what I’m doing.

Sometimes I’ll know I need to begin something and I’ll sort of circle around it. Like I’ll open the file, or put the document on my desk, or think, “Okay, I’m going to start that after I answer this one email,” and then somehow I’m still not actually starting the thing. But I don’t know if that’s what you mean, because it doesn’t always feel like I’m sitting there completely unable to move. It’s more like I’m trying to line myself up to begin, and the actual beginning keeps getting pushed a little farther away.

And then other times, if there’s a very clear first step, I can start fine. So it’s inconsistent, which makes it hard for me to describe. I wouldn’t say I never have trouble starting tasks, but I also don’t know if I can give you a simple yes without overexplaining it. It’s more like getting started can feel strangely slippery unless the task is already very concrete in my head.
Can you think of a time when you knew you needed to start a task but felt completely stuck, unable to take even the first step, not just delaying or circling around it?

I don’t know that I can honestly say “completely stuck” in that way. I’m trying to think of a clean example where I knew the task, understood the first step, and just could not make myself do even that first action, and nothing specific is coming to mind.

What I notice more is that I get kind of tangled up before the first step. Like, I might not be sure what the real first step is, or I feel like I need to organize the information first, or I’ll tell myself I should clear one small thing out of the way before I start. So from the outside it might look like I’m stuck, because the task isn’t moving. But inside it feels more like I’m trying to set up the conditions to start, if that makes sense.

There are definitely moments where I’ll sit there with something open and feel this resistance, like, “Ugh, I need to begin this,” but I don’t know if I’d describe it as being unable to take the first step. It’s more that I keep negotiating with myself about how to start, or when to start, or whether I need one more piece of information first.

So… no, I don’t think I have a clear example of being totally frozen at step one. It’s usually messier than that. I delay, I over-prepare, I hover around it, but I don’t know that I’ve experienced it as completely unable to do anything at all.
Can you think of times when you’ve had trouble keeping track of your belongings, staying organized, or remembering routine responsibilities, even when they weren’t related to work tasks?

Yes, that happens, and it’s not only work tasks. It’s more like… routine things that should be simple, and I fully intend to do them, but they somehow don’t stay in my mind at the right time.

For example, I’ll tell a junior staff member, “Yes, I’ll call you back this afternoon,” and I mean it when I say it. It’s not a vague promise. I’ll even have a reason to call them back, like they asked me something or needed guidance. But then the day moves on, and unless I’ve put it somewhere very obvious, I may realize later that evening or the next day that I never called. And then I feel awful, because it looks careless, but in my head it wasn’t that I dismissed them. It just slipped out of the active part of my mind.

Same with bills. I can know a bill is due and think, “I’ll pay that before the late fee hits,” and then somehow the fee hits. That one is especially frustrating because it’s so concrete. It’s not complicated. I have the money, I know how to pay it, I’m not trying to avoid it. I just don’t always remember at the correct moment, and then I’m irritated with myself because it feels like such an unnecessary mistake.

And calendars are another one. I’ve agreed to mentorship events and then not put them on my calendar right away. I’ll think, “Okay, yes, I’m doing that,” and because I’ve mentally agreed to it, it almost feels like I handled it. But if I don’t actually enter it in the calendar, it can just disappear until someone mentions it again or I see an email thread. Then I have this little jolt of panic, like, wait, did I ever record that anywhere?

So yes, routine responsibilities are definitely a problem sometimes. It’s not that I don’t care about them. It’s more that intending to do something and reliably capturing it in a way I’ll remember are apparently not the same thing for me.

patient.answer:
Yes, that happens, and it’s not only work tasks. It’s more like… routine things that should be simple, and I fully intend to do them, but they somehow don’t stay in my mind at the right time.

For example, I’ll tell a junior staff member, “Yes, I’ll call you back this afternoon,” and I mean it when I say it. It’s not a vague promise. I’ll even have a reason to call them back, like they asked me something or needed guidance. But then the day moves on, and unless I’ve put it somewhere very obvious, I may realize later that evening or the next day that I never called. And then I feel awful, because it looks careless, but in my head it wasn’t that I dismissed them. It just slipped out of the active part of my mind.

Same with bills. I can know a bill is due and think, “I’ll pay that before the late fee hits,” and then somehow the fee hits. That one is especially frustrating because it’s so concrete. It’s not complicated. I have the money, I know how to pay it, I’m not trying to avoid it. I just don’t always remember at the correct moment, and then I’m irritated with myself because it feels like such an unnecessary mistake.

And calendars are another one. I’ve agreed to mentorship events and then not put them on my calendar right away. I’ll think, “Okay, yes, I’m doing that,” and because I’ve mentally agreed to it, it almost feels like I handled it. But if I don’t actually enter it in the calendar, it can just disappear until someone mentions it again or I see an email thread. Then I have this little jolt of panic, like, wait, did I ever record that anywhere?

So yes, routine responsibilities are definitely a problem sometimes. It’s not that I don’t care about them. It’s more that intending to do something and reliably capturing it in a way I’ll remember are apparently not the same thing for me.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's presentation is most consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation, based on a chronic pattern of difficulty with task completion, organization, and forgetfulness in daily activities, which are core features of ADHD. Depressive and anxiety disorders were considered but ruled out due to lack of sustained mood symptoms or primary anxiety features.
